question: What are the six constraints of REST architecture?
title: The Six REST Constraints
direct_answer: REST has six constraints: Client-Server, Stateless, Cacheable, Uniform Interface, Layered System, and Code-On-Demand (optional). Together they define what makes a system truly RESTful.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know REST beyond just HTTP verbs and understand the architectural principles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Listing only 2-3 constraints or confusing REST with HTTP
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain how each constraint contributes to scalability and maintainability

sections.title: REST Architectural Constraints
sections.content: Roy Fielding defined REST in his 2000 dissertation with six architectural constraints. These aren't just guidelines—they define the REST architectural style. An API that violates these constraints isn't truly RESTful, even if it uses HTTP and JSON.

sections.title: The Six Constraints
content: 1. Client-Server: Separation of concerns — UI and data storage evolve independently
2. Stateless: Each request contains all information needed; server stores no client session state
3. Cacheable: Responses must define themselves as cacheable or non-cacheable (Cache-Control headers)
4. Uniform Interface: Standardized way to interact — resources, HTTP methods, self-descriptive messages, HATEOAS
5. Layered System: Client cannot tell if it's connected directly to the server or through intermediaries (load balancers, caches, gateways)
6. Code-On-Demand (optional): Servers can extend client functionality by sending executable code (JavaScript)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: REST has six architectural constraints defined by Roy Fielding. The most critical ones are: Stateless, meaning each request is self-contained; Uniform Interface, which gives REST its predictability; and Layered System, which enables scalability through load balancers and caches. The others are Client-Server separation, Cacheability, and the optional Code-On-Demand. In practice, most REST APIs focus heavily on statelessness and uniform interface—those are what interviewers typically probe.

followup_questions: Which constraint do you think is most important and why?
What is HATEOAS and why is it rarely implemented?
How does statelessness affect horizontal scaling?

question: Why is statelessness the most important REST constraint for scalability?
title: Statelessness and Scalability
direct_answer: Statelessness means the server stores no session data between requests. Every request carries its own authentication and context. This allows any server instance to handle any request, enabling horizontal scaling without sticky sessions.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding the real-world implications of REST constraints, not just memorization
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying stateless means the API has no state at all — the state lives in the client or database, not the server memory
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Connect statelessness to JWT tokens and load balancing in Spring Boot

sections.title: Why Statelessness Enables Scaling
sections.content: In a stateful architecture, the server remembers who you are between requests using server-side sessions (HttpSession). This means you must always hit the same server — called sticky sessions. With statelessness, authentication info travels with every request (via JWT, API key, or OAuth token), so any server in a cluster can handle the request.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Stateful: server stores session → must use sticky sessions or shared session store (Redis)
Stateless: client sends JWT/token with every request → any server can handle it
Load balancer can freely route requests to any instance
Server restarts don't invalidate sessions
Tradeoff: slightly larger requests (token overhead), server can't easily invalidate sessions without a token blacklist

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: Statelessness is key for scalability because it removes server-side session storage. When the server doesn't remember anything between requests, you can add more servers freely — a load balancer can route any request to any instance. In Spring Boot REST APIs, we achieve this with JWT tokens: the client sends the JWT in every Authorization header, so no server memory is needed. The tradeoff is that logout is harder since you can't just delete a server-side session — you need a token blacklist or short expiry times.

followup_questions: How do you handle logout in a stateless JWT-based system?
When would you choose stateful sessions over JWT?
What is a shared session store and when is it used?

question: What is the Uniform Interface constraint and what are its four sub-constraints?
title: Uniform Interface Sub-Constraints
direct_answer: Uniform Interface means all REST APIs interact the same way. Its four sub-constraints are: resource identification in requests (URIs), manipulation of resources through representations (JSON/XML), self-descriptive messages (Content-Type headers), and HATEOAS (hypermedia links).

interviewer_intent.testing: Depth of REST knowledge beyond surface-level understanding
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing HATEOAS exists or confusing it with pagination links
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Acknowledge that HATEOAS is rarely implemented in practice and explain why

sections.title: Uniform Interface Explained
sections.content: The Uniform Interface is what makes REST predictable and standardized. It means regardless of which REST API you use, the interaction model is the same: use URIs to identify resources, use HTTP methods to act on them, exchange JSON/XML representations, and (ideally) include hypermedia links.

sections.title: Four Sub-Constraints
content: 1. Resource identification: URIs uniquely identify resources (/users/123)
2. Manipulation through representations: JSON or XML body, not the resource itself
3. Self-descriptive messages: Content-Type: application/json tells client how to parse
4. HATEOAS: Response includes links to related actions — rarely implemented in real APIs

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Uniform Interface constraint has four parts. First, resources are identified by URIs. Second, clients interact through representations — you send and receive JSON, not the actual database record. Third, messages are self-descriptive through headers like Content-Type. Fourth, there's HATEOAS — Hypermedia as the Engine of Application State — where responses include links to next possible actions. In practice, most APIs skip HATEOAS because it adds complexity without enough benefit for typical use cases.

followup_questions: What is HATEOAS and why don't most APIs implement it?
How does Content-Type negotiate between JSON and XML?

question: What does the Layered System constraint mean and how does it enable enterprise architecture?
title: Layered System Constraint
direct_answer: Layered System means clients cannot tell whether they're communicating directly with the server or through intermediaries like load balancers, API gateways, or CDNs. Each layer only knows about the adjacent layer, enabling modularity.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding how REST fits into real-world infrastructure
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking this is just about code layers (controller/service/repo) rather than network topology
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Give examples: API Gateway, CDN caching, load balancer, reverse proxy

sections.title: What Layered System Means
sections.content: The Layered System constraint says the client doesn't need to know if it's talking to the actual server or an intermediary. A request from a mobile app might pass through: DNS → CDN → Load Balancer → API Gateway → Application Server. The client just sends an HTTP request and gets a response.

sections.title: Common Intermediary Layers
content: CDN: Caches static responses geographically close to users
Load Balancer: Distributes traffic across multiple server instances
API Gateway: Rate limiting, authentication, routing (AWS API Gateway, Kong)
Reverse Proxy: Nginx or Apache in front of Spring Boot app
Benefit: Each layer can be added/changed without client knowing

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Layered System constraint means the client only knows it's sending HTTP requests — it doesn't need to know if there's a load balancer, CDN, or API gateway between it and the actual application server. In a typical Spring Boot production deployment, your mobile app hits CloudFront for caching, then an AWS load balancer, then an API Gateway for auth and rate limiting, and finally your Spring Boot instance. The REST client is unaware of all these layers.

followup_questions: What is an API Gateway and what does it do?
How does CDN caching work with REST APIs?
What's the difference between a reverse proxy and a load balancer?

question: What is cacheability in REST and how do you control it with HTTP headers?
title: REST Cacheability and Cache-Control Headers
direct_answer: The Cacheable constraint requires REST responses to explicitly state whether they can be cached. This is done via Cache-Control, ETag, and Last-Modified headers. Caching reduces server load and improves response times.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding HTTP caching mechanics in REST APIs
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying REST APIs can't be cached because they're dynamic
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Cache-Control directives and ETag for conditional requests

sections.title: REST Cacheability
sections.content: The Cacheable constraint means every REST response must be labeled as cacheable or not. GET requests for product listings or user profiles can be cached. POST/PUT/DELETE are typically not cached. Proper caching dramatically reduces database load and API latency.

sections.title: Cache Control Headers
content: Cache-Control: max-age=3600 — cache for 1 hour
Cache-Control: no-cache — always revalidate with server
Cache-Control: no-store — never cache (sensitive data)
ETag: server sends hash of response; client sends If-None-Match on next request
304 Not Modified: server says cache is still valid
In Spring Boot: ResponseEntity.ok().cacheControl(CacheControl.maxAge(1, TimeUnit.HOURS)).body(data)

sections.title: How to Say It in an Interview
sections.content: The Cacheable constraint requires REST APIs to communicate caching intent through headers. For example, a product catalog endpoint might return Cache-Control: max-age=3600 to allow a 1-hour cache. For conditional caching, ETags let the client ask 'has this changed?' — if not, the server returns 304 Not Modified with no body, saving bandwidth. In Spring Boot, you use the CacheControl builder in ResponseEntity to set these headers. Sensitive endpoints like user data should use Cache-Control: no-store.

followup_questions: What is the difference between no-cache and no-store?
How do ETags work for optimistic concurrency?
What is CDN cache invalidation and when is it needed?
